newsitem.title: COTE D'IVOIRE: Ivorian president pledges war on corruption.
newsitem.headline: Ivorian president pledges war on corruption.

text.p: Ivory Coast President Henri Konan Bedie launched a landmark conference of his ruling Democratic Party on Monday, pledging to wage war on corruption and talking of opening his government to the opposition.

The 10th ordinary congress, which follows the party's 50th birthday in April, is the first ordinary conference not chaired by independence president Felix Houphouet-Boigny, who towered over the West African nation until his death in 1993.

Taking change as its theme, it has been billed as the first of the "Bedie era" -- which began on Houphouet's death but has taken shape since Bedie's election as president during a disputed 1995 poll coloured by political and ethnic violence.

"In the responsible democracy that we have chosen, the fight against corruption in all its forms is under way," Bedie told party militants decked out in orange patterned party shirts and dresses and vocal in their support for their leader.
"A state's credibility depends first of all on the exemplary behaviour of its representatives and civil servants at all levels, principally of its officials and its elected representatives," he said.

In a gesture to set aside the bitterness that surrounded his election in some quarters, he held out the prospect of a wider opposition role in government. "We envisage a wider opening of government to the opposition whether or not represented in parliament," he said.
The ruling party has 148 of the national assembly's 175 seats.

The opposition Ivorian Popular Front (FPI) and Rally of the Republicans (RDR) have 21 between them with six to be decided on December 29 -- three where polling was postponed in an opposition stronghold in a region where political and ethnic election violence killed 25 people.

Veteran FPI leader Laurent Gbagbo is standing for one of the three seats but neither Ivorian Workers Party leader Francis Wodie, the only opposition candidate to stand against Bedie in October 1995, nor RDR leader Djeny Kobina are assembly members.

Expropriation of public funds has been a problems in Ivory Coast, the world's top cocoa producer, since independence from France in 1960. In 1977, Houphouet-Boigny launched his own crusade against corruption.
After a post-independence economic boom the economy slipped into recession in the late 1980s but has revived since the 1994 devaluation of the CFA franc used in much of French-speaking Africa.
Growth in 1995 was seven percent, in part due to higher world commodity prices.

The government has launched an ambitious programme of economic liberalisation with the help of the World Bank and International Monetary Fund and is developing the oil and minerals sector and working to build industrial development on processing the nation's agricultural and mineral wealth.
